title: Research Bite #52: Three Types of Conceptual Change: Belief Revision, Mental Model Transformation, and Categorical Shift
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #52 draws on Michelene T. H. Chi's influential chapter 'Three Types of Conceptual Change: Belief Revision, Mental Model Transformation, and Categorical Shift,' a foundational piece in the conceptual-change literature widely cited in science-education research (published as part of the International Handbook of Research on Conceptual Change). Chi's framework distinguishes three 'grain sizes' of knowledge that conflicts with instruction: individual false beliefs, flawed mental models built from multiple related beliefs, and robust misconceptions rooted in category mistakes. The first two, Chi argues, can be fixed through direct refutation or the accumulation of corrected beliefs. Robust misconceptions -- the kind common in science, such as treating heat as a substance or force as inherent to moving objects -- are different in kind: they persist because the learner has assigned the concept to the wrong ontological category altogether (e.g., treating a process as a thing). Fixing these requires learners to become aware of the category error itself and to actively construct a new category, not simply absorb a corrected fact. Barton's framing for teachers is that not all misconceptions are equal, and treating a categorical misconception like a simple factual error will fail.
points: Chi's three-tier taxonomy -- false belief, flawed mental model, robust misconception -- gives teachers a diagnostic before they choose a correction strategy, rather than defaulting to 'just tell them the right answer' for every misconception.

The claim that robust misconceptions stem from category mistakes (not false facts) explains why repeated direct refutation often fails to shift deep-seated science misconceptions: the student's whole categorical framework, not just one belief, is wrong.

Fixing a categorical misconception requires the learner to become explicitly aware of the category error and construct a new category -- a demand that goes well beyond correcting a fact, implying instruction needs to name and confront the category itself.
Because most classroom feedback targets individual false beliefs, this framework suggests teachers may be systematically under-treating the hardest, most persistent misconceptions in science.

The distinction between 'adding new knowledge' and 'changing existing incorrect knowledge' reframes conceptual change as a spectrum of difficulty, not a single uniform process teachers can address with one technique.
quotes: The provided text explores three distinct types of conceptual change in learning, particularly within science education: belief revision, mental model transformation, and categorical shift. It distinguishes between learning that simply adds or completes prior knowledge and the more complex process of changing existing, incorrect ideas.
The author argues that false beliefs can be revised through direct refutation, and flawed mental models can be transformed by accumulating multiple belief revisions.

The text emphasizes that robust misconceptions, often found in scientific domains, necessitate a more profound categorical shift, where a concept is reclassified into a different lateral or ontological category due to a fundamental misunderstanding of its nature.
This deeper form of conceptual change requires learners to be aware of their category mistake and to build a new, appropriate category for understanding.

For robust misconceptions, teachers should understand they often stem from category mistakes, not just false beliefs. Refuting individual beliefs is often insufficient. Instead, instruction must aim for categorical shifts by making students aware of these fundamental errors and building new, appropriate categories.
